This is the part where I made my own second, minor error of the day. I initially told her that because she was using a cashier's check, the payment would credit to her available balance pretty much immediately, and that she should see same-day availability. That’s often true, but I spoke too soon. When I processed the corrected payment for $3,530.00, the system flagged it and placed a standard hold on the funds. An alert popped up on my screen. I had to backtrack and explain the situation to her, which is never my favorite thing to do. I apologized again and explained that my initial statement was incorrect, and that for certain check deposits, including cashier’s checks, the system automatically applies a hold to ensure the funds clear from the issuing bank. I reassured her this was a standard procedure and not a reflection on her or her account history. She asked how long the hold would be, so I showed her the confirmation screen. The funds from this specific payment are on hold until July 18, 2026. To give her more context, I explained that our policy for cashier's checks over $7,500.00 can sometimes involve even longer holds, so this was just the system operating as designed for a payment of this type. She was perfectly understanding. I printed out her receipt, highlighted the confirmation number BRC-4493749 for her, and made sure she had it for her business records.

It’s always fun when you connect with a customer about something other than banking.

The purpose of the visit was to apply the full amount of the check to her outstanding balance. I took the check and started keying in the transaction. I must have been thinking about the Herons' starting lineup or something, because I made a clumsy typo and entered the payment as $3,350.00. [2026-07-15 - 15:50 UTC | BRANCH_SUPPORT] BRANCH VISIT WRITE-UP (part 3/4)
This is the part where I made my own second, minor error of the day. I initially told her that because she was using a cashier's check, the payment would credit to her available balance pretty much immediately, and that she should see same-day availability. That’s often true, but I spoke too soon. When I processed the corrected payment for $3,530.00, the system flagged it and placed a standard hold on the funds. An alert popped up on my screen. I had to backtrack and explain the situation to her, which is never my favorite thing to do. I apologized again and explained that my initial statement was incorrect, and that for certain check deposits, including cashier’s checks, the system automatically applies a hold to ensure the funds clear from the issuing bank. I reassured her this was a standard procedure and not a reflection on her or her account history. She asked how long the hold would be, so I showed her the confirmation screen. The funds from this specific payment are on hold until July 18, 2026. To give her more context, I explained that our policy for cashier's checks over $7,500.00 can sometimes involve even longer holds, so this was just the system operating as designed for a payment of this type. She was perfectly understanding. I printed out her receipt, highlighted the confirmation number BRC-4493749 for her, and made sure she had it for her business records.

[2026-09-06 - 14:50 UTC | TELEPHONY_IVR] PHONE AGENT CALL TRANSCRIPT
IVR: Thank you for calling Chase Business Card Services. Your call may be monitored or recorded for quality assurance. For English, press one. Para Español, oprima dos. To continue in English, please remain on the line. Please say or enter the sixteen-digit card number you are calling about. If you do not have your card number, say 'I don't have it'.

IVR: I heard a noise in the background. Please say or enter your card number.

IVR: Okay. In a few words, tell me the reason for your call. You can say things like, 'check a balance', 'report a lost card', or 'dispute a transaction'.

IVR: I'm sorry, I didn't get that. Please tell me the reason for your call. You can say 'agent' at any time to speak to a representative.

IVR: Okay, transferring you to an agent. Please be aware that wait times may be longer than usual. Your business is important to us.

HOLD MESSAGE: Did you know you can earn even more with your Chase Ink Business card? Ask our agent about our latest offers, including an incredible 5x points on dining for a limited time. Don't just do business, do more business, with Chase.

AGENT: Thank you for holding, you've reached Chase Business Services, my name is Alex. How can I help you today?

CUSTOMER: Hi, yes, I hope you can. I’ve been having a terrible time with my card. It’s completely locked, I think.

AGENT: I can definitely look into that for you. I'm sorry to hear you're having trouble. First, I just need to verify your identity. Can I get your full name, please?

CUSTOMER: Hannah Nguyen. That’s H-A-N-N-A-H, Nguyen is N-G-U-Y-E-N.

AGENT: Thank you, Ms. Nguyen. And just for security, can you please confirm your date of birth?

CUSTOMER: It’s [REDACTED].

AGENT: Perfect, thank you. Just pulling up your account now. My system is being a little slow today, apologies. Classic Monday morning, even though it’s… what is it, Tuesday?

CUSTOMER: Ugh, tell me about it. It’s a hot one here in Phoenix today. Already feels like a furnace outside.

AGENT: I hear that. It’s actually pretty nice up here for once. We had that big storm last night but it’s cleared up. So, you’re in Phoenix? Did you catch the Granite Falls Miners game over the weekend? What a nail-biter.

CUSTOMER: Oh, we did! My wife was screaming at the TV. I can’t believe they pulled it out in the ninth.

AGENT: Right? I thought for sure they were done for. Okay, looks like my system is finally cooperating. Thank you for your patience. So, I’m looking at the Chase Ink Business Cash card ending in, uh, one-seven-nine-one. Is that the correct one?

CUSTOMER: Yes, star-one-seven-nine-one. That’s the one. It just… it stopped working. I was in Tokyo for a conference, I have a travel notice on file for that, and I tried to buy a train ticket and it was declined. Then I tried to add it to my phone wallet, and that didn't work either. It’s very embarrassing.

AGENT: Oh, I can certainly understand that would be frustrating, especially when you're traveling internationally. Let me see here. Okay, I’m looking at the account notes… just one moment while I read through this. Hmm. Okay. I see a few things here.

CUSTOMER: Okay…

AGENT: Right, so it looks like the system placed a security lock on the card on September fourth.

CUSTOMER: The fourth? Why? What happened?

AGENT: Well, our automated fraud detection system picked up on some unusual activity. It looks like there were two sign-in attempts to your online account, one from your home base in Phoenix, Arizona, and another one just a few minutes later from Miami, Florida.

CUSTOMER: Miami? I haven't been to Miami in years. That wasn't me.

AGENT: Okay, that’s what it looked like to the system. And right after that, there was a purchase attempted at a store in Miami… let’s see… Northgate Camera & Audio, for a pretty high amount. The first time it was declined and a text was sent to your mobile on file asking if it was a legitimate charge.

CUSTOMER: I… I think I remember that. I was in a meeting, I saw a text, and I just replied 'Y' because I thought maybe my wife, Renata, was buying something for the business. She’s on the account.

AGENT: I understand. Well, after that 'Y' reply, the charge was approved. But because of the strange login pattern—the two cities so close together—the system put an automated security lock on the card as a precaution, just to make sure nothing else could get through.

CUSTOMER: Oh my god. So that's why it was declined at H-E-B later that day? I tried to call in about that but I got stuck in the phone menu and hung up.

AGENT: Yes, I see a note about that call attempt as well. And that would also be why the transaction in Tokyo and the attempt to add the card to your Samsung Pay were declined. The note says the error was 'CARD_STATUS_LOCKED_RESTRICTED'. So the lock is definitely still active.

CUSTOMER: So… can you take it off? It was a mistake, I guess, that Miami charge. But the rest is me. I’m the one in Tokyo.

AGENT: I really wish I could, Ms. Nguyen. I can see your approved travel notice for Japan right here, so that all makes sense. However, because this lock was placed by our top-level Fraud and Security department, I don't actually have the tools to remove it myself. It's what we call a hard lock, and it requires a review from that specific team.

CUSTOMER: You’re kidding me. So I’m stuck without my primary business card?

AGENT: I’m so sorry. I know how inconvenient this is. What I need to do is open an escalation case for you. This will get all the information over to the Security team, and they'll be able to investigate and remove the lock. I can do that for you right now.

CUSTOMER: Okay… I guess that’s the only option.

AGENT: Yes, ma'am. Let me just get this started. Okay… just typing up the notes for them. I'm referencing the concurrent login, the charge in Miami, and your confirmation that the activity in Japan was legitimate. The case number for your reference is CASE-4677706.

CUSTOMER: Okay… CASE-4677706. Got it. So what happens now? Do they call me?

AGENT: They will. We can schedule a callback for you. That team works standard business hours, so what's the best date and number for them to reach you?

CUSTOMER: Uh, well I’m back in Phoenix now. Let’s see… Today is the seventh. Can they call on the tenth? September 10, 2026.

AGENT: Absolutely. September 10, 2026. And what’s the best number?

CUSTOMER: They can call my office landline. It’s 602-555-0195. Sorry, wait, I always do that. It’s 602-555-0159. The last two digits are five-nine.

AGENT: No problem at all. Let me just correct that. Okay, so I have a callback scheduled for you on September 10, 2026, to the number 602-555-0159. And that’s a landline, not a mobile, correct? We won't be able to text it.

CUSTOMER: Correct, it’s my office landline.

AGENT: Perfect. And listen, Ms. Nguyen, for all the trouble this has caused you, especially while you were traveling, I'd like to go ahead and apply a $20.00 courtesy credit to your account. I know it doesn't solve the problem right now, but I want to apologize for the inconvenience. Let me just try to process that for you... okay, one moment. While that’s loading, was there anything else I could help you with today?

CUSTOMER: Oh. Uh, wait, yes. Actually. While I have you. I was looking at my statement online when I was trying to figure all this out, and there’s another charge I don’t recognize at all.

AGENT: Okay, I can certainly help you with that. Can you give me the details?

CUSTOMER: Yeah, I have it right here. Um… at first I thought it was at Macy's? But no, that’s not it. Let me scroll… here. It’s for $190.14. The merchant says… Lakeview Pet Grooming?

AGENT: Lakeview Pet Grooming. And the amount was $190.14?

CUSTOMER: Yes, one-nine-zero-point-one-four. And it says it’s in Spokane, Washington. I have never been to Spokane in my life. We don’t even have a pet!

AGENT: Okay, I see that charge on my end as well. And just to confirm, you had your card in your possession on the date of that charge?

CUSTOMER: Yes, I did. I mean, my wife has her card too, but she was with me. Her card works fine, by the way, the one ending in 8616. This charge isn't on her card. It’s on mine. And neither of us made it.

AGENT: Understood. And you didn't authorize anyone else to use the card for this purchase?

CUSTOMER: No, definitely not.

AGENT: Okay, thank you for confirming. I'm going to file a dispute for this charge. It's a fairly standard process. We’ll credit the amount back to your account temporarily while we investigate with the merchant. Just let me fill out the form here. Let’s see… okay. It’s important to keep your account in good standing during a dispute, so just a general reminder from my script here, uh, that any undisputed balances should be paid on time to avoid interest, and late payments can incur a late fee of up to $40.00. That’s just a general notice.

CUSTOMER: Right, of course.

AGENT: Okay, I have filed that for you. The dispute reference number is DSP-8451719. I've filed it under our internal reason code DISPUTE_RC_13.3, which is for 'Card Not Present' fraud claims. You should see a temporary credit for the $190.14 post to your account within one to two business days.

CUSTOMER: Great. At least that’s something.

AGENT: Yes. Oh, and Ms. Nguyen, one last thing. I was trying to apply that $20.00 courtesy credit for you… and it looks like the system has rejected it. It seems I can't apply any manual credits while the main security lock is on the account. I am so, so sorry about that. I really thought it would go through.

CUSTOMER: Of course it did. It’s just been one of those weeks. It’s fine, don’t worry about it. Just… make sure that security team calls me.

AGENT: I have triple-checked the callback details. They will definitely be in touch. So, to recap: I've opened case CASE-4677706 for the security team to investigate and remove the lock on your card. They will call you at your office landline, 602-555-0159, on September 10, 2026. And I've also filed dispute DSP-8451719 for the $190.14 charge from Lakeview Pet Grooming in Spokane, WA, which you should see credited back temporarily. Your card ending in one-seven-nine-one does remain locked for now.

CUSTOMER: Okay. I guess that’s all we can do. Thank you for your help, Alex.

AGENT: You are most welcome, Ms. Nguyen. I’m sorry again we couldn't fully resolve it on this call. Thank you for your patience, and thank you for calling Chase. Have a good rest of your day.

CUSTOMER: You too. Bye.

[2026-07-15 - 15:50 UTC | BRANCH_SUPPORT] BRANCH VISIT WRITE-UP
Customer Hannah Nguyen came in just after the lunch rush today, maybe around 1:30 PM. Very pleasant interaction. She’s not from around here, mentioned she’s in town visiting her sister for a few weeks and was enjoying the slightly cooler weather we’re having, which made me laugh. She came over to my desk and I offered her a coffee from the new machine. She actually remembered the old one we had and said this new one is a huge improvement, which is exactly what I've been telling management. We chatted for a minute about her drive over to the Westgate Commons branch; she was coming from the north side of town and was surprised at how light the traffic was. I told her she got lucky.

We also got talking about the Bay City Herons, of all things. I was wearing my Herons pin and she noticed it right away. Turns out she’s a huge fan and follows all the games even though she lives out of state. We both think the new shortstop is a game-changer but we’re a little worried about the bullpen getting tired so early in the season. She’s optimistic, which was nice to hear. It’s always fun when you connect with a customer about something other than banking.

Anyway, she was here to make a pretty substantial payment on her Chase Ink Business Cash (*1791) card. She had a cashier's check with her and handed it over. The purpose of the visit was to apply the full amount of the check to her outstanding balance. I took the check and started keying in the transaction. I must have been thinking about the Herons' starting lineup or something, because I made a clumsy typo and entered the payment as $3,350.00. I was moving through the screens and just before I hit the final confirmation, I glanced down at the physical check on my desk to double-check. That's when I saw my mistake. My face must have given it away because she asked if everything was alright.

I laughed it off and apologized, pointing to the number on my screen and then the number on her check. I told her I’d accidentally transposed a couple of digits and that I’m glad I have a habit of checking everything three times. She was very nice about it, said not to worry. I voided the initial entry and started over, this time very deliberately keying in the correct amount of $3,530.00. I turned my monitor so she could see and had her confirm the amount was correct before proceeding. She gave me the thumbs up and we moved on.

This is the part where I made my own second, minor error of the day. I initially told her that because she was using a cashier's check, the payment would credit to her available balance pretty much immediately, and that she should see same-day availability. That’s often true, but I spoke too soon. When I processed the corrected payment for $3,530.00, the system flagged it and placed a standard hold on the funds. An alert popped up on my screen. I had to backtrack and explain the situation to her, which is never my favorite thing to do. I apologized again and explained that my initial statement was incorrect, and that for certain check deposits, including cashier’s checks, the system automatically applies a hold to ensure the funds clear from the issuing bank. I reassured her this was a standard procedure and not a reflection on her or her account history. She asked how long the hold would be, so I showed her the confirmation screen. The funds from this specific payment are on hold until July 18, 2026. To give her more context, I explained that our policy for cashier's checks over $7,500.00 can sometimes involve even longer holds, so this was just the system operating as designed for a payment of this type. She was perfectly understanding. I printed out her receipt, highlighted the confirmation number BRC-4493749 for her, and made sure she had it for her business records.

Just as she was gathering her things, she paused and said she had one more question. She asked about her wife, Renata. She wanted to know if she could also make a payment on Renata’s card for her while she was here. She mentioned the card ending was 9764. I had to explain our privacy policy, that I couldn't even look up Renata’s account, let alone process a payment from a third party, even a spouse. I told Ms. Nguyen that Renata would need to visit a branch herself with her ID, or that she could easily make the payment herself online or through the mobile app. She said she figured as much but thought she'd ask. She said she'd just tell Renata to handle it online when she got home. She thanked me for my help and for the coffee. We wished each other a good rest of the week and hoped the Bay City Herons would pull off a win this weekend.

Follow-up:
None required. Customer's payment was processed and all questions were answered. Customer was understanding about the funds hold and the policy regarding her wife's account. No further action is needed on my part.
